newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan reform package to aid stocks eventually.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan reform package to aid stocks eventually.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's economic reform package will boost stocks in the next six to 12 months although the near-term outlook remains weak, analysts said on Monday.

"The package focused on macro-economic issues and its impact would come in the mid term," said Ather Raouf, director of sales of Carr Mashriq, a brokerage house. "But the country's weak fundamentals will keep the sentiment depressed in near term."

Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz announced the package on Friday, that reduced general sales tax to 12.5 percent from 18, corporate tax to 30 percent from 33 and scrapped regulatory duty on imports of raw materials used in manufacturing goods for exports.
The International Monetary Fund welcomed the package and hoped it would provide the basis for adoption of an enhanced structural adjustment loan.
"Demand management of the last three years failed to revive the economy and in fact resulted in a gradual deterioration of the industrial sector," a Carr Mashriq research report said.
"The 1997 economic package seems to be an attempt to try exactly the opposite and focuses on reducing the rate-widening the base."

Raouf said the market had not responded with fervour to the announcement because the package did not include any short-term sentiment boosters for the capital market. "Then there are concerns about the impact of tax cuts on the deficit this year."
The Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) 100-share index ended 17.55 points lower at 1,598.94 in the afternoon's special session after the announcement of the package on Friday.
On Monday's provisional close, the index lost another 23.03 points to 1,575.91 on what dealers described as a technical correction.
The Carr Mashriq research report said the gross loss on revenues due to tax cuts would be around 44.2 billion rupees.
"This loss, however, does not factor in any production/ productivity gains, improvement in tax collections and cut-down in smuggling."
"While the net impact on revenue collection and deficit will be mildly negative in the very short run, the outlook for the medium term is positive," the report said.
